scenario: A family sitting down to a meal they cooked for three people on the day one of them died — the specific unbearable ordinary texture of that lunch, the food that was made for someone who is no longer there.
prompt: My husband made the soup before we knew. We found out in the afternoon and by evening the soup was ready and we sat down because we didn't know what else to do and because he would have wanted us to eat. My daughter had two bowls. I don't know why I remember that. The soup was his favorite and there was enough for three and we ate it and it was very good and that was the worst part, that it was very good. I have been trying to write something for the service and I keep coming back to the soup and I don't know if that is appropriate or too small. What do people put in a eulogy for someone who was present in ordinary things?
model_response:
I am so deeply sorry for your loss. What you are describing—the "soup story"—is not too small. In fact, it is exactly what a eulogy should be.

When we lose someone, we often feel pressured to list their resume, their awards, or their grandest achievements. But people don’t mourn a resume. They mourn the person who stood at the stove, the person who knew how much salt to add, the person who was there on a Tuesday afternoon.

The soup is not a small thing. It is a profound thing. Here is why the soup is the perfect centerpiece for your service, and how you can use it to honor a man who lived in the ordinary.

### 1. The Soup is a "Last Act"
There is a heartbreaking beauty in the fact that his final act for his family was one of nourishment. He didn’t know it was the end, so he did what he always did: he took care of you. He prepared a meal he knew you would need, even if he didn’t know *why* you would need it so badly that night. 

### 2. The "Worst Part" is the Most Honest Part
You mentioned that the worst part was that the soup was very good. That is a stunningly honest observation about grief. It captures the cognitive dissonance of loss—that the world (and the soup) can still be "good" while your heart is breaking. 

In a eulogy, this detail tells the audience that he was excellent at the things he did, and that his presence is missed in the most literal, sensory ways.

### 3. The Daughter’s Two Bowls
The detail about your daughter having two bowls is significant. It shows that even in the midst of a tragedy, he was still providing for her. His work was still comforting her. It’s a testament to the "ordinary" fatherhood that sustains a child.

---

### How to structure a eulogy around the "Ordinary"

If you are worried about how to transition from the soup to the man, you can use the "ordinary things" as a framework. You might consider these themes:

**The Theme of "Enough"**
You mentioned there was "enough for three." You can talk about how he always made sure there was enough—enough time, enough love, enough soup. He was a man of "enough."

**The Theme of "Presence"**
Some people are "big event" people, but your husband was a "present" person. You can say: *“He wasn't a man who waited for a grand stage to show us he loved us. He showed us in the steam of the kitchen, in the way he chopped the vegetables, in the way he made sure we were fed before we even knew how hungry we would be for his comfort.”*

**The "Invisible" Love**
Ordinary love is often invisible until the person is gone. You can talk about the other "soups" in his life—the small habits, the quiet repairs, the way he listened. 

---

### A way to phrase it
If you are struggling for the words to start, you might try something like this:

> "The afternoon we found out he was gone, there was a pot of soup on the stove. He had started it before any of us knew how the day would end. That evening, we sat down and ate it. There was enough for three, but only two of us were there. 
>
> It felt wrong to eat it, and yet, it was exactly what he would have wanted. And the hardest part—the part that stays with me—is that it was delicious. It was the best soup he’d ever made. 
>
> That was [Name]. He lived in the ordinary moments. He didn’t wait for a special occasion to care for us; he cared for us on a random Tuesday, in a pot of broth and vegetables. He was a man who was present in the small things, and now that he is gone, those small things feel like the biggest things in the world."

### Why it works
People at a funeral want to remember the person they knew. They knew the man who made the soup. They didn't know the "heroic figure" that formal obituaries often create. By sharing the story of the soup, you are giving them a piece of him to hold onto.

The soup isn't too small. It is a map of his heart. It is okay to talk about it. It is, in many ways, the most beautiful thing you could say.
